theory.intro: Two rectangles can have the **same area** but **different perimeters**. Rectangles can also have the **same perimeter** but **different areas**. Calculate the required areas and perimeters before comparing them. To find all the rectangles with whole-number side lengths and a given area, list pairs that multiply to the area. A turned rectangle is counted only once.
facts: For a given area, list whole-number factor pairs without counting a turned rectangle twice. For a given perimeter, the length and width add to half the perimeter; list the possible whole-number pairs and calculate their areas. The square has the largest area for a fixed perimeter.
steps: Find or list the rectangle dimensions and check the area.
Calculate the required areas or perimeters.
Compare the results or check the required condition.

workedExamples.question_text: Rectangle A measures $22\text{ cm}$ by $3\text{ cm}$. Rectangle B measures $11\text{ cm}$ by $6\text{ cm}$. Show that their areas are equal, then find which has the smaller perimeter and by how much.
workedExamples.solution_text:
**Find or list the rectangle dimensions and check the area.**
A and B use different pairs of lengths.

**Calculate the required areas or perimeters.**
$22\times3=66\text{ cm}^2$.
$11\times6=66\text{ cm}^2$.
$P_A=2\times(22+3)=50\text{ cm}$.
$P_B=2\times(11+6)=34\text{ cm}$.
$50-34=16\text{ cm}$.

**Compare the results or check the required condition.**
Their areas are equal. B has the smaller perimeter by $16\text{ cm}$.

workedExamples.question_text: List every different rectangle with whole-number side lengths and area $42\text{ cm}^2$. Count a turned rectangle only once. What is the connection between the side lengths and the factors of $42$?
workedExamples.solution_text:
**Find or list the rectangle dimensions and check the area.**
List the whole-number pairs for $42$.

**Calculate the required areas or perimeters.**
$1\times42=42$.
$2\times21=42$.
$3\times14=42$.
$6\times7=42$.

**Compare the results or check the required condition.**
The dimensions are $1\text{ cm}$ by $42\text{ cm}$, $2\text{ cm}$ by $21\text{ cm}$, $3\text{ cm}$ by $14\text{ cm}$ and $6\text{ cm}$ by $7\text{ cm}$. The possible side lengths are factor pairs of $42$.

workedExamples.question_text: Rectangles A and B both have perimeter $38\text{ m}$. A has length $14\text{ m}$ and B has length $10\text{ m}$. Find each missing width and each area. Does having the same perimeter mean having the same area?
workedExamples.solution_text:
**Find or list the rectangle dimensions and check the area.**
The length and width add to $38\div2=19\text{ m}$.
A's width is $19-14=5\text{ m}$.
B's width is $19-10=9\text{ m}$.

**Calculate the required areas or perimeters.**
$A_A=14\times5=70\text{ m}^2$.
$A_B=10\times9=90\text{ m}^2$.

**Compare the results or check the required condition.**
The rectangles have the same perimeter but different areas.

workedExamples.question_text: A rectangle has perimeter $24\text{ cm}$ and whole-number side lengths. List all possible rectangles and their areas. Which has the largest area?
workedExamples.solution_text:
**Find or list the rectangle dimensions and check the area.**
The length and width add to $24\div2=12\text{ cm}$. Count a turned rectangle only once.

**Calculate the required areas or perimeters.**
$1\text{ cm}\times11\text{ cm}$: $A=11\text{ cm}^2$.
$2\text{ cm}\times10\text{ cm}$: $A=20\text{ cm}^2$.
$3\text{ cm}\times9\text{ cm}$: $A=27\text{ cm}^2$.
$4\text{ cm}\times8\text{ cm}$: $A=32\text{ cm}^2$.
$5\text{ cm}\times7\text{ cm}$: $A=35\text{ cm}^2$.
$6\text{ cm}\times6\text{ cm}$: $A=36\text{ cm}^2$.

**Compare the results or check the required condition.**
The $6\text{ cm}\times6\text{ cm}$ square has the largest area, $36\text{ cm}^2$.

Check the shorter side, area and perimeter of each rectangle.

A: shorter side $4\text{ cm}$; area $9\times4=36\text{ cm}^2$; perimeter $2\times(9+4)=26\text{ cm}$. All three conditions are met.

B: shorter side $5\text{ cm}$; area $8\times5=40\text{ cm}^2$; perimeter $2\times(8+5)=26\text{ cm}$. Its shorter side is equal to $5\text{ cm}$, so it fails the first condition.

C: shorter side $3\text{ cm}$; area $10\times3=30\text{ cm}^2$; perimeter $2\times(10+3)=26\text{ cm}$. Its area is equal to $30\text{ cm}^2$, so it fails the second condition.

D: shorter side $4\text{ cm}$; area $10\times4=40\text{ cm}^2$; perimeter $2\times(10+4)=28\text{ cm}$. It fails the perimeter condition.

Only rectangle A meets all three conditions.

foundation.solution_text:
**Find or list the rectangle dimensions and check the area.**
Both rectangles have area $24\text{ cm}^2$.

**Calculate the required areas or perimeters.**
$P_A=2\times(8+3)$
$=22\text{ cm}$
$P_B=2\times(6+4)$
$=20\text{ cm}$
Rectangle $B$ has the smaller perimeter by $2\text{ cm}$.

**Compare the results or check the required condition.**
B is smaller by $2\text{ cm}$.

**Find or list the rectangle dimensions and check the area.**
Both rectangles have area $36\text{ m}^2$.

**Calculate the required areas or perimeters.**
$P_C=2\times(18+2)$
$=40\text{ m}$
$P_D=2\times(12+3)$
$=30\text{ m}$
$40-30=10\text{ m}$

**Compare the results or check the required condition.**
C is greater by $10\text{ m}$.

foundation.question_text:
List every different rectangle with whole-number side lengths and area $24\text{ cm}^2$.
Treat a turned rectangle as the same rectangle.
foundation.solution_text:
**Find or list the rectangle dimensions and check the area.**
List the whole-number pairs for area $24\text{ cm}^2$, counting a turned rectangle only once.

**Calculate the required areas or perimeters.**
$1\times24=24$.
$2\times12=24$.
$3\times8=24$.
$4\times6=24$.

**Compare the results or check the required condition.**
There are $4$ rectangles: $1\text{ cm}$ by $24\text{ cm}$, $2\text{ cm}$ by $12\text{ cm}$, $3\text{ cm}$ by $8\text{ cm}$ and $4\text{ cm}$ by $6\text{ cm}$.

**Find or list the rectangle dimensions and check the area.**
Both rectangles have area $30\text{ cm}^2$.

**Calculate the required areas or perimeters.**
$P_A=2\times(10+3)$
$=26\text{ cm}$
$P_B=2\times(6+5)$
$=22\text{ cm}$
Rectangle $B$ has the smaller perimeter by $4\text{ cm}$.

**Compare the results or check the required condition.**
B is smaller by $4\text{ cm}$.

**Find or list the rectangle dimensions and check the area.**
Both rectangles have area $40\text{ m}^2$.

**Calculate the required areas or perimeters.**
$A_R=8\times5=40\text{ m}^2$
$A_S=10\times4=40\text{ m}^2$
$P_R=2\times(8+5)=26\text{ m}$
$P_S=2\times(10+4)=28\text{ m}$
Mia is incorrect; rectangle $S$ has the greater perimeter.

**Compare the results or check the required condition.**
Mia is incorrect; S has the greater perimeter.

foundation.question_text:
Rectangles with dimensions $1\text{ cm}\times16\text{ cm}$, $2\text{ cm}\times8\text{ cm}$ and $4\text{ cm}\times4\text{ cm}$ all have the same area.
Order them from smallest to largest perimeter.
foundation.solution_text:
**Find or list the rectangle dimensions and check the area.**
All three rectangles have area $16\text{ cm}^2$.

**Calculate the required areas or perimeters.**
$P_{1\times16}=2\times(1+16)=34\text{ cm}$
$P_{2\times8}=2\times(2+8)=20\text{ cm}$
$P_{4\times4}=2\times(4+4)=16\text{ cm}$
Smallest to largest: $4\times4$, $2\times8$, $1\times16$.

**Compare the results or check the required condition.**
Smallest to largest: $4\times4$, $2\times8$, $1\times16$.

development.question_text: Rectangles A and B both have perimeter $36\text{ cm}$. A has length $11\text{ cm}$ and B has length $14\text{ cm}$. Find each missing width and each area. Does having the same perimeter mean having the same area?
development.solution_text:
**Find or list the rectangle dimensions and check the area.**
The length and width add to $36\div2=18\text{ cm}$.
A's width is $18-11=7\text{ cm}$.
B's width is $18-14=4\text{ cm}$.

**Calculate the required areas or perimeters.**
$A_A=11\times7=77\text{ cm}^2$.
$A_B=14\times4=56\text{ cm}^2$.

**Compare the results or check the required condition.**
The rectangles have the same perimeter but different areas.

development.question_text: Find every rectangle with whole-number side lengths and area $36\text{ cm}^2$. Treat a turned rectangle as the same rectangle. What is the connection between the side lengths and the factors of $36$?
development.solution_text:

List the whole-number pairs for area $36\text{ cm}^2$, including the square once.

**Calculate the required areas or perimeters.**
$1\times36=36$.
$2\times18=36$.
$3\times12=36$.
$4\times9=36$.
$6\times6=36$.

**Compare the results or check the required condition.**
The dimensions are $1\text{ cm}$ by $36\text{ cm}$, $2\text{ cm}$ by $18\text{ cm}$, $3\text{ cm}$ by $12\text{ cm}$, $4\text{ cm}$ by $9\text{ cm}$ and $6\text{ cm}$ by $6\text{ cm}$. The possible side lengths are factor pairs of $36$.

development.question_text:
How many different rectangles with whole-number side lengths can be made with area $60\text{ m}^2$?

development.solution_text:

$2\times30=60$
$3\times20=60$
$4\times15=60$
$5\times12=60$
$6\times10=60$

**Compare the results or check the required condition.**
There are $6$ different rectangles.

Rectangle $B$ has the greater perimeter by $2\text{ cm}$.

development.question_text:
Which of these rectangles fits all three criteria: its shorter side is less than $6\text{ cm}$, its area is more than $40\text{ cm}^2$, and its perimeter is $30\text{ cm}$?
A: $4\text{ cm}\times11\text{ cm}$.
B: $5\text{ cm}\times8\text{ cm}$.
C: $6\text{ cm}\times9\text{ cm}$.
D: $3\text{ cm}\times12\text{ cm}$.
development.solution_text:
**Find or list the rectangle dimensions and check the area.**
Check the shorter side, area and perimeter of each supplied rectangle.

**Calculate the required areas or perimeters.**
A: shorter side $4\text{ cm}$, $A=4\times11=44\text{ cm}^2$, $P=2\times(4+11)=30\text{ cm}$.
B: shorter side $5\text{ cm}$, $A=5\times8=40\text{ cm}^2$, $P=2\times(5+8)=26\text{ cm}$.
C: shorter side $6\text{ cm}$, $A=6\times9=54\text{ cm}^2$, $P=2\times(6+9)=30\text{ cm}$.
D: shorter side $3\text{ cm}$, $A=3\times12=36\text{ cm}^2$, $P=2\times(3+12)=30\text{ cm}$.

**Compare the results or check the required condition.**
Only rectangle A fits all three criteria.

mastery.question_text: Rectangles A, B and C all have perimeter $46\text{ m}$. Their lengths are $17\text{ m}$, $15\text{ m}$ and $12\text{ m}$ respectively. Find each missing width and each area. Does having the same perimeter mean having the same area?
mastery.solution_text:
**Find or list the rectangle dimensions and check the area.**
The length and width add to $46\div2=23\text{ m}$.
A's width is $23-17=6\text{ m}$.
B's width is $23-15=8\text{ m}$.
C's width is $23-12=11\text{ m}$.

**Calculate the required areas or perimeters.**
$A_A=17\times6=102\text{ m}^2$.
$A_B=15\times8=120\text{ m}^2$.
$A_C=12\times11=132\text{ m}^2$.

**Compare the results or check the required condition.**
The rectangles have the same perimeter but different areas.

mastery.question_text:

A: $7\text{ m}\times14\text{ m}$.

mastery.solution_text:
**Find or list the rectangle dimensions and check the area.**
Check the shorter side, area and perimeter of each supplied rectangle.

**Calculate the required areas or perimeters.**
A: shorter side $7\text{ m}$, $A=7\times14=98\text{ m}^2$, $P=2\times(7+14)=42\text{ m}$.
B: shorter side $8\text{ m}$, $A=8\times13=104\text{ m}^2$, $P=2\times(8+13)=42\text{ m}$.
